https://www.parl.ca/DocumentViewer/en/14.tldr: The Building Canada Strong Act makes changes to federal laws to speed up project evaluations, especially for nuclear, energy, and transportation projects. It also streamlines labor rules, supply chain management, and environmental protection regulations.
https://www.parl.ca/DocumentViewer/en/14.summary:
This bill updates several Canadian laws to make the process for reviewing and approving large projects more efficient. It changes how impact assessments are conducted, particularly for projects regulated under the Nuclear Safety and Control Act and the Canadian Energy Regulator Act. It sets stricter time limits for these reviews to provide more certainty for project developers while still requiring that environmental impacts and Indigenous rights are considered. Furthermore, it gives federal ministers more authority to coordinate various permits and approvals to reduce delays. 

Beyond project approvals, the bill introduces reforms to Canada's supply chain management, including creating a new council to monitor trade corridors. It also updates labor laws under the Canada Labour Code to improve collective bargaining and payment enforcement for workers. Finally, it includes changes to maritime and transportation laws to help handle emergencies, digitalize trade documents, and better manage federal ports.
key_changes: It requires the Canadian Nuclear Safety Commission to lead impact assessments for projects involving nuclear activities.
It mandates that most federal impact assessments and energy project reviews must be completed within one year of receiving necessary information.
It creates a new framework for 'regions of national interest' to allow for faster project approvals within specific geographic areas.
It provides the Minister of Transport with new powers to coordinate reviews for major transportation projects and designate important trade routes.
It updates the Canada Labour Code to create new rules for collective bargaining and to help workers collect unpaid wages more easily.
It modernizes international trade by allowing for digital trade documents instead of requiring physical paper records.

https://www.parl.ca/DocumentViewer/en/14.tldr: The Wartime Service Recognition Act creates a new, transparent system for the government to officially recognize certain military missions as wartime service. This process uses specific risk-based criteria rather than relying on past labels assigned to those missions.
https://www.parl.ca/DocumentViewer/en/14.summary:
This bill requires the Minister of National Defence to develop a national framework that sets clear rules for what qualifies as 'wartime service.' This framework must be based on the actual risks and conditions soldiers faced during their service, such as exposure to violence or life-threatening situations, rather than how the mission was originally labeled. The Minister must also consult with veterans and military experts when creating these rules.

Once the framework is in place, the government will use it to formally designate specific military operations as wartime service. The bill also mandates the creation of a public, searchable list on the Department of National Defence website to track these operations. Importantly, this official recognition is symbolic and commemorative in nature; it does not change or add to any financial benefits that veterans or members are already entitled to receive.
key_changes: The Minister of National Defence is required to create a new national framework to define and recognize wartime service.
Wartime service will be decided based on specific risk factors and conditions on the ground instead of historical mission labels.
The government must publicly report on the framework and explain how it was developed through consultations with veterans and experts.
A new, searchable public list of military operations and their designation status will be maintained on the government website.
The Minister must conduct a formal review of all Canadian Armed Forces operations occurring since July 27, 1953, to see which qualify under the new rules.
This legislation provides a formal way to recognize service, but it does not provide any new or additional financial benefits to veterans.

https://www.parl.ca/DocumentViewer/en/14.tldr: This bill sets national rules for provinces to follow if they want to receive federal funding for mental health, addiction, and substance use services. It ensures these services remain accessible and fair across Canada.
https://www.parl.ca/DocumentViewer/en/14.summary:
The Mental Health Parity Act creates a set of national standards that provincial health insurance plans must meet to qualify for federal cash contributions. These standards cover public administration, the range of services provided, equal access for all residents, and coverage for residents moving between or temporarily outside of their home provinces. The goal is to ensure that mental health and addiction services are treated with the same requirements as general medical services under the Canada Health Act.

If a province fails to meet these standards—or if they allow extra-billing (charging patients extra for insured services) or user charges—the federal government has the authority to reduce or withhold their cash funding. The bill also includes a formal process for the federal Health Minister to investigate issues, consult with provincial counterparts, and report annually to Parliament on how well these standards are being met across the country.
key_changes: Provinces must now follow specific federal rules regarding mental health and addiction services to receive full federal funding.
Provincial insurance plans must be publicly administered and operate on a non-profit basis.
Services must be provided on equal terms to all eligible residents to ensure fair and universal access.
Provinces are prohibited from allowing extra-billing or user charges for insured mental health and addiction services.
The federal government can deduct money from provincial funding if they fail to meet these requirements or allow unauthorized charges.
The Health Minister is required to produce an annual report for Parliament on how provinces are complying with these new standards.

https://www.parl.ca/DocumentViewer/en/14.tldr: This bill temporarily pauses federal fuel taxes until January 31, 2027, and then cuts those taxes in half for February and March 2027. It applies to everyday fuels including gasoline, diesel, and aviation fuel.
https://www.parl.ca/DocumentViewer/en/14.summary: The Canadian Fuel Affordability Act amends the Excise Tax Act to provide temporary relief from federal taxes on fuel. These rules apply to unleaded gasoline, diesel fuel, aviation fuel, and both leaded and unleaded aviation gasoline.  First, the bill extends the existing pause on federal fuel taxes for any fuel taxes that become payable up until January 31, 2027. This part of the law is treated as having taken effect on September 8, 2026.  Second, starting February 1, 2027, and ending March 31, 2027, the taxes return at half their normal rates instead of coming back all at once. During this two-month transition, tax rates of 10 cents, 11 cents, and 4 cents are reduced to 5 cents, 5.5 cents, and 2 cents respectively.
key_changes: The suspension of federal fuel excise taxes is extended through January 31, 2027.
The rule extending the fuel tax pause is considered to have taken effect on September 8, 2026.
Federal excise taxes on fuels are cut to 50 percent of their regular rates from February 1, 2027, to March 31, 2027.
Specific fuel tax rates are temporarily reduced from $0.10 to $0.05, from $0.11 to $0.055, and from $0.04 to $0.02.
The tax relief applies to unleaded gasoline, diesel fuel, aviation fuel, and both leaded and unleaded aviation gasoline.
The half-rate fuel tax rules officially take effect on February 1, 2027.

https://www.parl.ca/DocumentViewer/en/13.tldr: This bill reduces federal barriers to trade and worker mobility between provinces, and creates a streamlined federal approval process for major projects deemed to be in Canada's national interest.
https://www.parl.ca/DocumentViewer/en/13.summary:
The first part of the bill focuses on free trade and worker mobility within Canada. It establishes that goods and services that satisfy provincial or territorial rules will generally be treated as meeting comparable federal standards for interprovincial trade. It also requires federal regulators to recognize provincial or territorial occupational licenses, allowing certified workers to obtain federal authorization to practice their trades and professions across Canada.

The second part introduces a fast-track system for major infrastructure, energy, and economic development projects identified as being in the national interest. For designated projects, required federal reviews and regulatory findings are legally presumed to be in favor of letting the project proceed. Instead of securing numerous separate federal permits, a project proponent can be granted a single ministerial document containing specific conditions that acts as all necessary federal authorizations.

To ensure transparency and safety, the bill requires consultations with provinces, territories, and affected Indigenous peoples, along with mandatory national security checks on foreign investments from hostile countries. Critical laws—including the Criminal Code, the Canada Labour Code, and the Indian Act—cannot be bypassed or altered. Additionally, the government must publish a public online registry showing project timelines, estimated costs, environmental studies, and explanations for why any regulatory recommendations were rejected.
key_changes: Goods and services that comply with provincial or territorial requirements are considered to meet comparable federal standards when moving between provinces.
Federal regulatory bodies must recognize provincial and territorial professional credentials and issue certified workers the federal authorizations needed to practice their occupation.
The federal government can designate major economic, energy, and infrastructure initiatives as national interest projects to fast-track their regulatory review.
The designated minister can issue a single project document that combines all required federal permits and sets out binding conditions the developer must follow.
A public online registry must be created to openly share each project's description, timelines, costs, environmental studies, and reasons for accepting or rejecting agency recommendations.
Key federal statutes, including the Criminal Code, the Indian Act, and the Canada Labour Code, are entirely exempt and cannot be bypassed or altered for any project.

https://www.parl.ca/DocumentViewer/fr/13.tldr: Cette loi vise à faciliter le commerce entre les provinces, à aider les travailleurs à pratiquer leur métier partout au pays et à accélérer la réalisation de grands projets jugés importants pour le Canada.
https://www.parl.ca/DocumentViewer/fr/13.summary: La première partie de la loi cherche à réduire les obstacles qui empêchent les produits, les services et les travailleurs de circuler librement d'une province à l'autre. Elle prévoit que si un produit ou un service respecte les règles d'une province, il sera aussi accepté au niveau fédéral. De même, un travailleur ayant le droit d'exercer sa profession dans une province pourra obtenir une reconnaissance pour travailler partout au pays.
key_changes: Les produits et services qui respectent les règles d'une province sont désormais considérés comme conformes aux règles fédérales.
Les professionnels autorisés à travailler dans une province peuvent obtenir une autorisation équivalente pour travailler ailleurs au Canada.
Le gouvernement peut désigner certains projets comme étant d'intérêt national pour les faire avancer plus rapidement.
Un ministre peut délivrer un document unique qui remplace plusieurs autorisations nécessaires pour ces grands projets nationaux.
Le gouvernement doit obligatoirement consulter les provinces et les peuples autochtones avant d'approuver ces projets d'intérêt national.
Un examen indépendant annuel doit être réalisé pour vérifier l'avancement et le respect des budgets de ces grands projets.

https://www.parl.ca/DocumentViewer/en/14.tldr: This bill officially recognizes November as National Immigration Month across Canada every year.
https://www.parl.ca/DocumentViewer/en/14.summary:
The National Immigration Month Act is a short piece of legislation designed to set aside a specific time each year to acknowledge immigration. By passing this bill, the government officially names November as National Immigration Month.

This designation applies to the entire country. The purpose is to ensure that every year, Canada observes this month as a way to recognize the role of immigration in the nation.
key_changes: The Act establishes November as the official National Immigration Month.
This recognition will occur annually across all of Canada.
The bill creates a formal national observance for immigration.
No specific events or government actions are mandated by this text.
The designation applies to every province and territory in Canada.

https://www.parl.ca/DocumentViewer/en/14.tldr: The Stopping Supply to Save Lives Act increases prison sentences and restricts parole for individuals involved in the trafficking, production, or movement of certain synthetic opioids.
https://www.parl.ca/DocumentViewer/en/14.summary:
This bill updates Canada's laws to create stricter punishments for those dealing with specific synthetic opioids. It sets mandatory life sentences for various drug-related crimes depending on the amount of the substance involved and updates the rules for when someone can be released from prison early, known as parole.

Additionally, the bill introduces new "aggravating factors," which are circumstances that allow a judge to give a harsher sentence. Judges must now consider it a more serious crime if these drug offenses occur near schools, child care facilities, or treatment centers, or if the amount of drugs involved is high enough to likely cause death.
key_changes: Anyone found guilty of trafficking or producing more than 40mg of a synthetic opioid will face a mandatory life sentence.
Individuals convicted of trafficking or producing specific amounts of synthetic opioids will not be eligible for parole for at least 25 years.
Crimes committed within 300 metres of schools, child care centers, or addiction treatment facilities are now legally defined as more serious offenses.
Judges must consider it an aggravating factor if the amount of the drug involved is enough to potentially kill a person.
The government is given the authority to designate additional protected locations where drug offenses will be treated more severely.
Minimum prison sentences of 15 years are established for offenses involving between 20mg and 40mg of synthetic opioids.
